title: Network security groups, application security groups and effective rules
learningObjective: Create NSGs and ASGs, associate them with subnets and NICs, predict whether a given flow is allowed, and prove it with effective security rules and IP flow verify.

prerequisites.text: VNets, subnets and private IP addressing
TCP/UDP ports and the idea of a stateful firewall

foundation: A network security group (NSG) is a list of allow and deny rules that Azure checks for traffic going into or out of a subnet or a single network interface (NIC).
Each rule has a priority number. Azure reads the rules from the lowest number to the highest and stops at the first rule that matches. That one rule decides the outcome.

Every NSG already contains default rules: traffic inside the virtual network is allowed, Azure Load Balancer health probes are allowed, and everything else coming in is denied. Outbound internet traffic is allowed by default.
You can attach an NSG to a subnet, to a NIC, or to both. When both exist, traffic must pass both of them.
An application security group (ASG) is a label you put on VM network interfaces (for example 'web' or 'db'). Rules can then say 'allow 1433 from web to db' instead of listing IP addresses.
engineer: Processing order: inbound traffic is evaluated by the subnet NSG first and then by the NIC NSG; outbound traffic is evaluated by the NIC NSG first and then the subnet NSG. A deny at the first level means the second level is never consulted.

Custom rule priorities range from 100 to 4096. Default rules use 65000 (AllowVnetInBound / AllowVnetOutBound), 65001 (AllowAzureLoadBalancerInBound / AllowInternetOutBound) and 65500 (DenyAllInBound / DenyAllOutBound). Default rules cannot be deleted but can be overridden by a higher-priority (lower number) custom rule.

Matching is a 5-tuple: source, source port, destination, destination port and protocol (TCP, UDP, ICMP or Any). Sources and destinations can be IP prefixes, service tags (Internet, VirtualNetwork, AzureLoadBalancer, Storage.WestEurope …) or ASGs.

NSGs are stateful. If an inbound flow on 443 is allowed, the response traffic is allowed automatically; you do not write a matching outbound rule. Existing flows are not interrupted immediately when a rule changes for connections already established.
The VirtualNetwork service tag covers the VNet address space, peered VNets and on-premises ranges connected through a gateway, so AllowVnetInBound is wider than many people assume.
A Standard SKU public IP is secure by default: inbound traffic is blocked unless an NSG on the subnet or NIC allows it. (Basic SKU public IPs were open by default and were retired in September 2025.)
ASG rules require that all NICs in an ASG are in the same virtual network, and a rule that uses ASGs on both source and destination requires both ASGs to be in that same VNet.

Effective security rules (portal: VM > Networking > Effective security rules, or Get-AzEffectiveNetworkSecurityGroup) merge the subnet and NIC NSGs and expand service tags into prefixes. The VM must be running to read effective rules. Network Watcher IP flow verify tests one 5-tuple and returns the deciding rule.

animation.caption: Send packets from the internet to a VM and watch each NSG level evaluate them rule by rule.

example.title: Three-tier app without IP lists
body: Contoso runs web VMs and SQL VMs in separate subnets of vnet-prod. Their NICs are tagged with ASGs asg-web and asg-db.

The subnet NSG for snet-web allows TCP 443 from Internet to asg-web (priority 200). The subnet NSG for snet-db allows TCP 1433 from asg-web to asg-db (priority 200) and denies TCP 1433 from VirtualNetwork (priority 300) so that only web servers reach SQL, even though AllowVnetInBound would otherwise allow every VNet source.
When the web tier scales out, new NICs join asg-web and inherit the rules. Nobody edits IP prefixes.

prerequisites: A resource group and a VNet with subnets
NSG and its VNet/NIC must be in the same region and subscription
permissions: Network Contributor (or Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/* ) to create and edit NSGs
Microsoft.Network/networkSecurityGroups/join/action to associate an NSG with a subnet or NIC
Microsoft.Network/virtualNetworks/subnets/write on the subnet when associating at subnet level
limits: Custom rule priority 100–4096; default limit of 1000 rules per NSG
One NSG per subnet and one per NIC; one NSG can be associated with many subnets and NICs
ASGs: NICs in one ASG must belong to the same VNet
portal: Network security groups > Create: choose subscription, resource group, name and region.
Open the NSG > Inbound security rules > Add: Source = Service Tag 'Internet', Destination = Application security group 'asg-web', Service = HTTPS, Action = Allow, Priority = 200.
NSG > Subnets > Associate: choose vnet-prod / snet-web.
VM > Networking > Application security groups > Configure: add asg-web to the NIC.
VM > Networking > Effective security rules (VM must be running) to verify the merged result.
Network Watcher > IP flow verify to test a single flow and read the deciding rule.
configuration.cli:
az network nsg create -g rg-web -n nsg-web-subnet -l westeurope
az network asg create -g rg-web -n asg-web -l westeurope
az network nsg rule create -g rg-web --nsg-name nsg-web-subnet -n Allow-HTTPS-Web \
  --priority 200 --direction Inbound --access Allow --protocol Tcp \
  --source-address-prefixes Internet --destination-asgs asg-web --destination-port-ranges 443
az network vnet subnet update -g rg-web --vnet-name vnet-prod -n snet-web --network-security-group nsg-web-subnet
az network nic ip-config update -g rg-web --nic-name vm-web-01-nic -n ipconfig1 --application-security-groups asg-web
az network nic list-effective-nsg -g rg-web -n vm-web-01-nic
az network watcher test-ip-flow -g rg-web --vm vm-web-01 --direction Inbound --protocol TCP \
  --local 10.0.1.4:443 --remote 203.0.113.10:50123
configuration.powershell:
$asg  = New-AzApplicationSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName rg-web -Name asg-web -Location westeurope
$rule = New-AzNetworkSecurityRuleConfig -Name Allow-HTTPS-Web -Priority 200 -Direction Inbound -Access Allow `
          -Protocol Tcp -SourceAddressPrefix Internet -SourcePortRange * `
          -DestinationApplicationSecurityGroup $asg -DestinationPortRange 443
$nsg  = New-AzNetworkSecurityGroup -ResourceGroupName rg-web -Name nsg-web-subnet -Location westeurope -SecurityRules $rule
$vnet = Get-AzVirtualNetwork -ResourceGroupName rg-web -Name vnet-prod
Set-AzVirtualNetworkSubnetConfig -VirtualNetwork $vnet -Name snet-web -AddressPrefix 10.0.1.0/24 -NetworkSecurityGroup $nsg | Set-AzVirtualNetwork
Get-AzEffectiveNetworkSecurityGroup -NetworkInterfaceName vm-web-01-nic -ResourceGroupName rg-web

lab.objective: Diagnose why SSH and HTTPS fail to reach vm-web-01, then fix the configuration with the smallest change.
steps: Send an HTTPS (443) packet with only the default rules in the subnet NSG and observe which rule denies it.
Add an inbound Allow rule for TCP 443 from Internet with priority 200 and resend.
Enable the NIC NSG (it has only default rules) and resend HTTPS. Explain why it now fails again.
Add the same allow rule to the NIC NSG, or remove the NIC NSG, and confirm the packet arrives.
Send SSH (22) and confirm it stays blocked: least privilege.
expected: HTTPS initially denied by DenyAllInBound (65500) in the subnet NSG.
After the fix, allowed by your priority-200 rule.
With a NIC NSG containing only defaults, denied again at the NIC level.

validation.text: Observed a packet denied by DenyAllInBound
Allowed HTTPS with a custom rule
Observed a NIC-level deny after the subnet allowed the packet

failureScenarios: Priority 4000 allow placed below a priority 300 deny: the deny wins.
Allow rule written as Outbound instead of Inbound.
Rule targets port 3389 while the client connects on 22.
cleanup: Simulation only: use Restart to reset the rule set.
lab.cost: None. Runs entirely in the browser.

troubleshooting.symptom: Cannot RDP/SSH to a VM with a public IP; no NSG errors visible.
troubleshooting.cause: Standard SKU public IP and no NSG allowing the port: secure by default.
troubleshooting.fix: Add an inbound allow rule for the port (preferably from your IP only), or better, use Azure Bastion.

troubleshooting.symptom: Subnet NSG allows 443 but the site still times out.
troubleshooting.cause: A NIC-level NSG denies the traffic (inbound passes subnet first, then NIC).
troubleshooting.fix: Check Effective security rules on the NIC; align or remove the NIC NSG.

troubleshooting.symptom: Database reachable from every subnet despite a 'web only' rule.
troubleshooting.cause: AllowVnetInBound (65000) allows all VirtualNetwork sources; your allow rule does not restrict others.
troubleshooting.fix: Add an explicit deny for the port from VirtualNetwork with a priority below 65000 but after the ASG allow.

troubleshooting.symptom: Effective security rules are greyed out.
troubleshooting.fix: Start the VM, or use IP flow verify from Network Watcher.

troubleshooting.symptom: Load balancer backend marked unhealthy after adding a deny-all rule.
troubleshooting.cause: A custom deny at a priority lower than 65001 blocks the AzureLoadBalancer health probe source.
troubleshooting.fix: Add an allow from the AzureLoadBalancer service tag above the deny.

comparisons.difference: Central, stateful, fully managed firewall with FQDN filtering, threat intelligence and logging; NSGs are distributed 5-tuple filters at subnet/NIC level. They are complementary.
Attach to ENIs and contain allow rules only (no deny, no priority). NSGs support both allow and deny with priorities.
Stateless subnet filters with numbered rules; NSGs are stateful.

misconceptions.myth: The rule with the most specific match wins.
misconceptions.reality: Priority order wins. The first matching rule by lowest priority number decides, regardless of how specific later rules are.

misconceptions.myth: You need an outbound rule for responses to allowed inbound traffic.
misconceptions.reality: NSGs are stateful; return traffic for an allowed flow is permitted automatically.

misconceptions.myth: A subnet NSG allow overrides a NIC NSG deny.
misconceptions.reality: Both levels must allow inbound traffic. Either one can block it.
Default rules cannot be removed; you override them with lower-numbered custom rules.

architectureDecisions: Prefer subnet-level NSGs as the baseline and avoid NIC NSGs unless a VM needs an exception; two layers double the troubleshooting surface.
Use ASGs instead of IP lists so autoscaled VMs pick up rules automatically.
Do not open 22/3389 to the internet; use Azure Bastion or just-in-time VM access.

Application security groups and service tags

steps.label: Open ports
steps.title: Every port open to everyone
body: A VM with RDP open to the internet is attacked within minutes. You need a firewall at the network level.

steps.label: Rules
steps.title: How an NSG rule works
body: Each rule has a priority (100–4096, lower number is checked first), source, destination, protocol, port range and action (Allow or Deny). The first matching rule wins; later rules are ignored. NSGs are stateful: replies to allowed traffic are allowed automatically.

steps.label: Defaults
steps.title: Default rules you cannot delete
body: Inbound: allow within the VNet (65000), allow the Azure load balancer (65001), deny everything else (65500). Outbound: allow within the VNet, allow the internet, deny everything else. Override them with lower-numbered rules.

callout.text: Default inbound denies the internet. Default outbound allows the internet.

steps.label: Two NSGs
steps.title: Subnet and NIC NSGs together
body: You can attach an NSG to a subnet and another to a NIC. Inbound traffic is checked by the subnet NSG, then the NIC NSG; outbound in the reverse order. Both must allow it.

callout.text: Effective security rules shows both together.

steps.label: ASGs
steps.title: Rules by role, not by IP
body: An application security group (ASG) is a label for NICs, such as asg-web. Use ASGs as rule sources and destinations: 'asg-web may reach asg-db on 1433'. New VMs just join the ASG. Service tags (Internet, VirtualNetwork, Storage, AzureLoadBalancer) stand for Microsoft-managed ranges.

steps.label: Recap
steps.title: NSGs
body: Lowest number first; both NSGs must agree.
recap: Defaults: deny inbound internet, allow outbound internet
Subnet then NIC inbound; NIC then subnet outbound

handsOn.title: Write NSG rules with an ASG and read the effective rules
handsOn.cost: Low. One B1s VM costs about US$0.01 per hour. Delete the same day.
before: Signed in at portal.azure.com as Owner of a subscription (a free or pay-as-you-go account works). Work in a resource group called rg-az104-lab.
If rg-az104-lab does not exist yet: search 'Resource groups' > Create > name rg-az104-lab, region UAE North (or any region near you) > Review + create > Create.

A virtual network vnet-lab (10.10.0.0/16) in rg-az104-lab with a subnet snet-app (10.10.1.0/24): Virtual networks > + Create > IP addresses tab. For these labs, untick 'Enable private subnet' on snet-app so lab VMs can reach the internet (in production use a NAT gateway instead).

A small Linux VM vm-lab in snet-app of vnet-lab: Virtual machines > + Create. Image Ubuntu 24.04, size Standard_B1s, password authentication, Networking tab: vnet-lab / snet-app, public IP: None, NIC network security group: Basic, public inbound ports: None. If the VM cannot reach the internet later, its subnet is private (the default for new networks): open the virtual network > Subnets, untick 'Enable private subnet', save, then stop and start the VM. In production use a NAT gateway instead.

steps.do: Search 'Application security groups' > + Create. Group rg-az104-lab, name asg-web, region UAE North (or any region near you). Create.
Open vm-lab > Networking > Application security groups > Add application security groups > asg-web. Save.
steps.see: asg-web listed on the VM's NIC.

steps.do: Open the VM's NIC NSG (vm-lab-nsg) > Inbound security rules > + Add. Source: Any, destination: Application security group asg-web, port 80, TCP, Allow, priority 200, name allow-http-web. Add.
Add another rule: destination asg-web, port 80, TCP, Deny, priority 100, name deny-http-test.
Open Network Watcher > IP flow verify: vm-lab, inbound, TCP, local port 80, remote IP 198.51.100.1, port 40000.
steps.see: Denied by deny-http-test: priority 100 is checked before 200.

steps.do: Delete deny-http-test and run IP flow verify again.
Create an NSG nsg-subnet in rg-az104-lab and associate it with snet-app (NSG > Subnets > Associate). Run IP flow verify again.
steps.see: Denied: the subnet NSG has only default rules, so it blocks port 80 before the NIC NSG is checked.

steps.do: Open vm-lab > Networking > Effective security rules.
steps.see: Two sections, one for the subnet NSG and one for the NIC NSG.

check: You saw priority order and the two-NSG rule in action.
cleanup: When you finish for the day: Resource groups > rg-az104-lab > Delete resource group > type the name > Delete. This removes everything inside it.
